My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) puts a good deal of stress upon an arrangement in this matter. I had no arrangement myself, except that a certain document was handed to me after some talk with the hon. gentleman. One of its terms is the adoption of existing permanent lists if there are any such in the respective provinces to which the women's names have been added. If there is any bad faith about this thing it is not mine.
It is not mine, because I never furnished any such document as that.

I do not think there is any bad faith on the part of any body.
I was one of those to whom the proposed legislation was submitted, and there was no arrangement in regard to it. I admit that I myself offered suggestions; some of them were accepted, others were refused.
I have never said that I would be bound to accept the legislation in whole or in part. We have simply tried to make it more acceptable, if possible.

Everything that my hon. friend from Kamouraska says is absolutely true, Mr. Chairman. He has tried and we have all tried-I have tried to make this as acceptable ds I could. I think I can call on my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) to confirm that. I realize the difficulties under which we are all labouring and I want to make this list as fair as I possibly can. In our committee meetings we balked entirely without reserve. I have felt all day that a lot of this discussion might have been avoided.

There is nothing I abhor and despise so much as a person making, an agreement and not keeping it. It has been hinted that we have made an agreement and have not lived up to it. Here is a document sent to me by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House in which this is stipulated:
That where there are permanent lists finished and completed in the province, they shall he accepted, and probably this rule will apply to Nova Scotia and British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
Might I say a word? In this Bill we have carried out the principle that where there are existing provincial lists not more than one year old, those lists are accepted. There is this provision added, that where those lists do not contain the names of all persons within* the constituency in which a by-election is to be held, machinery is to be provided whereby the names of those persons may be added to those lists. The only object we have in view is not to disfranchise any one. If the lists were nine months old, I think every one would agree there might be a number of persons in the constituency whose names would not be on those closed lists. All we have done in the case of Nova Scotia is to accept those lists and devise machinery whereby there may be added the names of persons who are qualified and not now on those lists. I think every person will agree that that principle is fair and right. There may be some objection to the machinery provided, but I think I may say in all, fairness that we have endeavoured in the best way we could under

somewhat trying circumstances to devise machinery that would prevent the exclusion from the lists of any persons who are qualified to vote; and, personally, I am inclined to the view that we have succeeded pretty well.

Lest there should be some misunderstanding in connection with this committee, in addition to the explanation already given, let me say that so far as I am aware there was no hard-and-fast committee. Certain members on both sides of this Hoqse conferred together and discussed certain terms of the measure. I, as one of the members of that conference, very much appreciate the action taken, which I might suggest, if exercised oftener, would tend to advance legislation, and, perhaps, contribute to a better feeling in the House. The point raised by my hon. friend from Anti-gonish (Mr. Sinclair) I think I have personal knowledge of, by reason of the fact that it was not discussed when he happened to be in the room; that is, all the members who took part in the conference did not happen to be present at all the sessions or all the time. Those who took part, no matter what were their views on the legislation, finished the conference with their views unchanged as to the principle of the Bill. A great many of the changes suggested were accepted by the members representing the Government, some were not, and those members who held the opinions upon which those- suggestions were based hold them still-
And reserve the right to hold them still.
Yes, as the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough stated; and there is no bad faith in giving expression to those opinions to-day.
Section agreed to.

I would like to go back to section 6, subsection (1). If my hon. friend would refer to the end of that subsection he will see it reads:
Or in any air service, or while acting as a war correspondent in connection with any war in which any military, naval or air forces of Canada are or have been serving.
I would move to amend the subsection by adding:
Provided that no such person shall he qualified to be enumerated os an elector or to vote at an election unless he has been for the period of one month a resident of the district in which the election is held.
That would be the whole electoral district -the county, or whatever it might be.
Suppose a soldier has just returned home?
It would not apply at all, because 'he would not have lost hi3 residence.
Many of these soldiers have no homes. Why not let them vote wherever they happen to toe?
There may be a few scattering exceptions, but as a rule every soldier had a home before he left Canada.
A great many had no residence.

My 'hon. friend will understand that practically every man has a place of residence somewhere, and wherever he enlisted he had a residence. He never loses that; even if gone five years, he still has that residence.

Thousands of soldiers enlisted at places far from where they were living. Take the Northwest, many men were working far from Edmonton and Calgary who enlisted in those cities. Take my own home town, the battalion formed there was made up to a great extent of men working in the next county. The only point I make is: Why not let the soldier vote wherever he happens to toe?

I do not think that a fair proposition. We are trying to make this an honest law. There is a difference of opinion as to how to do it, but I think it was in the mind of every person to see if we could not provide a law, fair and honest law, that will allow every man to vote who has the right to vote. Let us assume a by-election in North Ontario,-not far from my hon. friend's constituency. Some person wanting to be dishonest could bring in five hundred or a thousand soldiers the day before the polling.
I have heard of its being done.

I do not think my hon. friend would want that, and I do not think any man in this House would want it. But if a man has been a resident there for a month, he becomes a resident as a matter of fact and should have the right to vote.
The returned men are not soldiers now.

I know of fifty soldiers in my home town, mostly from the Northwest, who are visiting their friends

there; the same in North Ontario. Why should they not be allowed to vote there, although their homes are in the Northwest?
They are not residents there.
A labouring man has no residence.
Under this amendment, if he moved into North Ontario, with the intention of residing there, after a month he would have the right to vote.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 10-polling divisions and voters' lists for the several divisions:

I move:
That the word " due " be inserted after the word' " in " in line 44 of section 10.

Is there any provision in this Bill under which the returning officer is obliged to put up notices as to where the poll is to be held? I was put in a very difficult position at the last election because of the fact that the returning officer in a neighbouring town did not put up any notice, and refused to tell us where the poll was going to be held. It was in the short days of December, and as the poll opened at six o'clock in the morning all my friends could do was go out and follow the men who were proceeding to the poll by lantern light. The intention was to open the poll without any of my agents being present and then to refuse to swear them. That is the advantage which was taken of the War-time Elections Act on that occasion.

I assure my hon. friend that we are preserving the old law as it has been on the statute book practically since Confederation. We are not working under the War-time Elections Act-I would hope not, too. We are getting back to the old law under which notices must be given and such procedure has as my hon. friend has been used to all his lifetime.

On section 11-voters' lists in polling divisions in cities and towns in places with over
1,000	population:

There are incorporated towns with less than a population
of 1,000. Would they be regarded as polling districts?

I would think not.-If 1
could have had this section drafted as I wanted it, I would have had it read " in cities and incorporated towns." So far as conditions in Eastern Canada are concerned, that would be the proper way to draft the section; but we are told that that would not be impracticable in Western Canada. A great many of the incorporated towns there have a population of not more than 300, 400 or 500, and the result would be that you would be providing for the registration system in these small com-muuities where there ought to be the enumeration system. It was decided, therefore,	to draft the	section as itnow stands. Then,	somebody	had
to decide what places should come under the principle of registration, and what places^ should come under the principle of enumeration. I do not know that some better scheme might not have been devised, but it was thought that the Secretary of State would, be in the best position to determine whether a place is a city or town and whether it has a population of over 1,000 persons.

Take the town of Bad-deck; no one can tell where it really begins or ends. It is a little village, a shire-town, and it spreads out and thins out until you get to the farms. If I had to make a delimitation of the boundaries of the town, I could hardly do so.
Is the town of Baddeck incorporated?

No. It is sipply one of those towns which may or may not have a population of 1,000; it is not incorporated. It is part of the municipal district of Baddeck; the town itself and a large area around it constitutes a polling division.

As I understand this section, Baddeck would certainly not come within the registration system; it would be enumerated. This only applies to cities and incorporated towns, or those places which, under the provincial laws are cities and incorporated towns, "and" which have a population of one thousand or over.
If that is the case, there is not so much objection.

The section'reads1:
In polling divisions wholly or partly contained within places having a population of more than one thousand persons and which places are. under the provincial law, cities or towns, the



voters' lists shall be prepared and completed under a personal registration system and the rules and directions set forth in Schedule B to this Act shall apply.	,
Does that mean, according to the last decennial census?

I think that would be a matter of fact. That is why the Secretary of State was designated as the person who should decide, whether the place should come under the registration system or under the enumeration system.
That would involve the taking of a census.

No; the Secretary of State would have the last census to go by, and he would have also the usual data which are in the statistical office at Ottawa. I see no better way of working it out than to leave it to the Secretary of State.
I think it would be better if the word "incorporated" was added before the word "cities" in line 4 of this section.
I would prefer to have it read "cities or incorporated towns."
Perhaps that would be better.
Is not a town an incorporated organization?

I will give my hon.
friend a very outstanding case, in New Brunswick; I refer to the town of Sackville, where there are about 3,000 people who are living in what we call a town, but it never was incorporated, and for municipal purposes and for election purposes, it takes in a large area of country territory. Therefore, it would be a hard matter to draw a distinction. But if you use the words " incorporated town " there would be no question at all that Sackville would not be included. I move to insert the word " incorporated " before the word " towns " in the fourth line of this clause.

Amendment agreed to, and subsection as amended agreed to.

On section 15-persons on voters' list entitled to vote:

There appears to be
some idea that, although you take a complete list, taking my province for instance, it is the intention that some names can be struck off. I strenuously object to any power being given to strike off any name once it has been regularly put on.

The three subclauses
IS, 14 and 15 refer to the municipal portions of constituencies, that is, the portions which are enumerated and not registered, and there is no striking off in the enumeration, because no matter what the list may be that is placed in the returning officer's hands, any person who is qualified to vote can go to the poll on election day and, if his or her name is not on the list, can demand the right to be sworn and his or her vote is deposited in the ballot box. So that my hon. friend will see that the erasure has no effect whatever. When I read subclause 15 first, I thought it might be construed to mean that only the persons whose names were on that particular voters' list had a right to vote, and I had an amendment drafted and, indeed, I have the draft here. But when I came to examine into the thing a little more carefully, I was satisfied that the subclause was properly drafted. Subclause 13, practically at the end reads:
And, such oath having- been taken, the deputy returning officer shall at once cause such person's name to be added to the voters' list, with the word sworn written thereafter, and subject to the two next following sections of the Act. such person may thereupon vote.
The idea is this. When a man goes into the polling booth and his name is not upon the list and he demands the right to be sworn, the moment he is sworn his name is added to the list, so that before he can vote his name is on the list. Once his name is on the list he can be challenged on account of residence, on account of bribery-he is subject to all the challenges that any voter would be subject to. It means that, as soon as he is sworn, his name gets on the list, and then subclause 15 provides that all persons whose names are on the lists have the right to vote.
Does that apply to registration?
No, only to enumeration. As regards registration, the lists are closed four days before the election.	.

Subsection agreed to.
On subsection 21-penalty for registrar, etc., falsely signing, etc., statutory declaration to be used for registration of voters:

Is there any provision in this Bill for penalizing any official, enumerator, registrar or any other election official, who may be guilty of fraudulent or criminal conduct under the law? In our provinces, the revisers and people who make up the lists are subject to a very severe penalty if they do anything wrong; anything to disfranchise a person. Is there any provision whereby any election official who may lend himself to irregularities or malfeasance in office can he penalized?
Mr. CARVE,LL: Let me give an illustration. There is a certificate, form JJJ, on page 21, which reads:
I certify that the foregoing is a true copy or
the voters' list in polling division No	
(or as the case may he) of the electoral district of	as prepared
hy me for use in the election of a member (or members, as the case may be) of the House of Commons for the said electoral district, now pending.
That is the enumerator's certificate. This subsection provides that if he makes a false statement or false oath, he is 'subject to a penalty. In addition to that, all the penalties under the old election law are still maintained. That law is not changed in the least particle from what it has always been. There has just been placed in my hands a proposed amendment by the Prime Minister to the subsection dealing with the voting of women of foreign
birth, which I will read so that hon. gentlemen may consider it during the dinner hour. The amendment is that a further section be added to the Act as follows:
3. In the case of such a bye-election, clause (c) of subsection 2 of section 1 of Chapter 2<0 of the Acts of 1918, An Act to confer the Electoral Franchise on Women, shall not apply.
Hon. gentlemen will observe that we have introduced the principle that a woman of foreign birth will be allowed to vote by obtaining a certificate from a judge that she is possessed of the necessary qualifications entitling her to naturalization. It seems to me, in view of the amendment we have made this afternoon to subsection 2 of section 5, a certain portion of the Franchise Act of 1918 conferring the franchise on women should be repealed. Otherwise there, would be a conflict, because the provision we have' inserted in this Bill is not exactly ,in accordance with the provisions of section 1, chapter 20 of the Acts of 1918.
I am not just sure also that we have not made a mistake in inserting the word "incorporated" before the word "town." I am afraid that might lead to our having the system of enumeration followed in some very large places where there should be registration. The system of enumeration, of course, can be a great engine for wrong if used except in rural communities. I do not think you could ever work out an enumeration system which would be anything like a protection against fraud in a large city where people do not know one another well. The theory of the enumeration system is that in the country districts everybody knows everybody else, and it is almost impossible for fraud to be perpetrated. The town of Sackville occurred to me while I was thinking this over. Sackville is not an incorporated town, but yet it has about 3,000 people, and some factories and industries; people might be coming into that town to work right along. If the word "incorporated" is left in, that town would have to be enumerated and not registered.
In other words, it is an actual town, although not a legal town.

I wish the minister would consider during recess the proclamation part of the amendment moved by the Prime Minister to subsection 2 of section 5. I am getting to be a very old lawyer, but I find it very hard to understand that proclamation, and I am not sure whether the ordinary layman would understand what it really means.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

After Recess.
The Committee resumed at seven-thirty o'clock.

I was in error in moving to insert the word " incorporated " in sections 11, 12 and 13. They had better be left as they are, as there might he less danger of confusion. Chapter 20 of the Act of 1918 provides the qualifications entitling a woman to vote. She must be a British subject, twenty-one years of age, possessing the qualifications necessary, and for the purpose of the Act shall be deemed a British (Subject, etc. There is a provision that she must obtain a certificate from a judge of a court of record stating that she possesses qualifications which would entitle her to naturalization. In this Bill we are going over the same thing providing qualifications for the woman voter, using different language. I move that we add a new section 3 to the Bill as follows:
3. In the case of such a bye-eleotion, clause (c) of subsection 2 of section 1 of Chapter 20 of the Acts of 1918, an Act to confer the Electoral Franchise on Women, shall not apply.
Does this mean that the provisions in that Act are not required because you have other provisions?
We have included provisions in this Bill for the same thing, but they are somewhat different.
This phraseology refers only to the provisions of that Act and not to women voting?

Yes. There was a clause with regard to women of foreign birth obtaining the certificate which gave them the right to vote. We have changed that and made it a little broader than in the Act of 1918, and for that reason it is better to repeal the Act of 1918 and incorporate the provisions in this.

Section agreed to.
On schedule " B ", subsection 5:
Why not say, a relative within a certain degree? You do not want a Scotch cousin.
Or an "unmarried wife."
In the same paragraph further down strike out the letter " s " in the .word " persons " and make it singular.

Amendments agreed to, and subsection as amended agreed to.
On subsection 11 of Schedule B.
My hon. friend (Mr. Cal-der) has a proposition which I think is agreed to by all parties.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization

speechtext: Except in the city of Montreal and the city of Quebec, where there are, in Quebec, a chief justice, and in Montreal, an acting chief justice, there are no senior judges.
Yes, in Sherbrooke.
And in Three Rivers.
In all the other districts there is no senior.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: If there is only one, he will be the senior. It will not be any one else.
Are you going to make a change about the registrar acting as* clerk ?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: That is struck out.

With regard to the expression " senior County Court judge," that is all right in Ontario, because there are senior County Court judges, hut in the other provinces there are no senior County Court judges. You may reason it out that way, hut I do not think it is very good drafting to talk about a senior judge, when there is only one.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: You might put in "the senior County Court judge or the County Court judge."
And it will be the same about the Superior Court judge.

It is better drafting to leave it as it is. If there is only one judge, he is the senior judge. In different provinces we have different conditions. In Ontario, we have, in many counties, two judges, one called the senior and the other called the junior.
Because there are two.
Because there are two. In other cases there is only one. If you use the word "senior" you use the proper word.
Why should we do a stupid thing by talking about a senior judge, when there is only one judge?
In my judgment, the other would be the stupid thing.
It fits in Ontario, because in many counties there are two judges, but in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, there is only one.

There has 'been quite a change made in section 11. The Bill as printed provides that the registrar shall act as clerk of the revising officer. The amended section does not provide that; it provides that the revising officer may appoint a clerk. Therefore, I suggest that that should be, struck out, and that the revising officer should appoint his own clerk.

He was in the same position at the time of the election in 1917. He acted in Cape Breton where he lived, but he had to appoint another man in Victoria county. There might toe a case where a man might have to go a long distance before he got before a court of record to

be sworn. He is sworn before the Superior Court.

That will be the case in my own constituency. On the other hand, without very mature consideration, I would rather maintain it as it is, for this reason. These are pretty important officers, they are taking the place .of a judge. I think they should go to the judge, who appoints them, even it means half a day's ride on a railway train, and should be sworn by him and instructed, in order to make them realize the importance of the duties they are going to perform.

Consideration oi amendments made by the Senate to Bill No 160, to amend the Criminal Code.-The Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Many of the amendments made by the Senate are of a minor character. The first one is in subclause 2 of clause 1, which reads:
Any property, real or personal, belonging or suspected to belong to an unlawful association, or held or suspected to be held by any person for or on behalf thereof may, without warrant, be seized or taken possession of by any person thereunto authorized by the Chief Commissioner of Dominion Police, and may thereupon be forfeited to His Majesty.
The Senate have added, after the word " Police " the words " or by the Commissioner of the Northwest Mounted Police," that force having police judisdiction in western Canada. The next amendment made by the Senate is to strike out the minimum penalty of one year's imprisonment in each ease.
They leave no minimum, but they leave the maximum at twenty years The next is a similar amendment making the Commissioner of the Northwest Mounted Police of equal authority with the Chief Commissioner of Dominion Police in respect of subclause 4 of the new section 97B. The next amendment changes the number of days within which an accused person may elect speedy trial. The Senate have made it thirty days before trial instead of forty, and they have changed our fifty days to forty. 1 think it will make the effect of the amendments more clear if I read the clause as it stood, and as it will stand if these 
amendments are agreed to. The clause as ft passed this House read:
And provided also that no prisoner shall have a right to re-elect later than forty days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the eourt at which trials by jury can be had, unless the prisoner was committed for trial within fifty days' 'before the said date, in which event he must re-elect not later than ten days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at which trials by jury can be had.
As amended by the Senate it will read:
And provided also that no prisoner shall have a right to re-elect later than thirty days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at which trials by jury oan be had, unless the prisoner was committed for trial within forty days before the said date, in which event he must re-elect not later than ten days before the day fixed for the next sittings of the court at which trials by jury can be had.
They have followed the very same principle as we sought to embody in the law, but they have gone a little further than we did. They have gone up to thirty days of trial instead of forty days; consequently, they have allowed only forty days for demand for trial, whereas we allowed fifty.
Is "re-elect" the proper word?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is how it was
drafted in the'first place. I presume it must be the right word.
Suppose a prisoner elects to go to the Supreme Court. He has the right afterwards to " re-elect " to be tried by jury.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then " re-elect " will be the right word, according to the explanation of my hon friend.
This does not change the old conditions of electing in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.
To what does the fifty days refer?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As it passed this House, if a man were committed earlier than fifty days before the trial he had to make his election for speedy trial, or re-election, as it would be more properly called, before forty days previous to the trial. The Senate amendments provide tnat if he is committed before forty days for trial he must make his re-election earlier than thirty days before trial.

By the expression " before trial " does the minister mean before the meeting of assizes at which the trial will be held?

Mr. MEIGHHEiN: Yes, that would be the more correct expression. Then section 16 as the Bill left this House provided for the Act coming into effect 90 days after assent. The Senate have amended it to bring the Act into effect on the first of October next.
I see no substantial objection to any of the Senate amendments, and I therefore move that they be concurred in.
Motion agreed to, and concurred in.

Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 177, to amend the Judges' Act-Mr. Meighen.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice) f The Senate has made two amendments to, this Act. As both amendments have relation in a certain sense to revenue, and as on that account there might possibly be some doubt as to the propriety-I fancy not the constitutionality-of the amendments being made in the Senate, I might explain that they were made at my suggestion. It will be remembered that at the last moment an amendment was made in this House providing that the exemption as to taxes and deductions that had been provided for in the Judges' Act should not apply in the case of any judges whose salaries were not increased by the Bill. I had in mind at that time that the increases of salaries were $1,000, and did not have in mind that in the case of Prince Edward Island there were three increases, two of them only for $300, and the other for $500. In the case of the $300 increase I fear we shall be taking out more with the left hand than we put in with the right, because the whole income is to be taxable. Consequently, the amendment that was suggested and was adopted by the Senate was to limit the class of judges whose salaries are now being made taxable to those whose salaries are increased by this Act by more than $500.
The other amendment made by the Senate has the effect of restoring the allowance for divorce for the judges in divorce in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. As the Bill passed this House these allowances for judges in divorce were eliminated.
Special judges have been appointed known as judges in divorce in these two provinces only. The reason the Bill was introduced and allowed-so far as I was concerned-to pass in that form was that I anticipated the passage in this House of the Divorce Bill by which jurisdiction in
divorce would have been given to all Superior courts. Consequently, there was no reason why any special allowance should be made to any special judge for acting in divorce proceedings. But inasmuch as that Bill has not passed, there is no reason to justify the taking away of the salary that has always been paid to those judges for that work, because those judges alone have jurisdiction in divorce and do all the work in divorce as well as their share of the work of the higher court in other matters. Therefore the Senate restores the salary in each case to the judge of divorce in New Brunswick and the judge of divorce in Nova Scotia. The allowance to each is $500, just as in the past. The amendment makes the section read:
The first five lines of section 9 of said Act are repealed and the following substituted therefor; ; and so on.
By repealing only the first five lines the divorce allowance remains in the old Act.
What does the judge in Nova Scotia get?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In Nova Scotia I believe the judge is Mr. Justice Ritchie. He is not Chief Justice. He receives $7,000 with the allowance of $500. The same applies to Judge Crockett in New Brunswick.

There is another anomaly which I had hoped the minister would observe. We did not touch the salaries .of the Superior judges in Ontario and Quebec. Now the judges of the other provinces are on the same footing with those, but we have the anomaly that the judge in Manitoba pays income tax on the whole of his salary and his confrere in Ontario pays nothing. That is an extraordinary condition.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the suggestion was first made it appealed to me to be of some force, though possibly not compelling force, but I was immediately answered by the member for Shelburne and Queens to the effect that we had already passed the income tax and made the -salary of the judge appointed from now on taxable, while his confrere sitting beside him was receiving a non-taxable salary.

They should all be
taxed or not taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I thought there was as much force in the answer as in the objection and consequently I think it should stand at that. I move that the House con-

our in the amendments made by the Senate to the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION AND AUTHORITY OF THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
There is none, and that is the reason why the statements made by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) and repeated by the leader of the Opposition are incorrect. The Order in Council authorized the Controller to "conduct an inquiry into and concerning the manufacture, sale, price and supply of newsprint paper within the Dominion of Canada. I am now referring to the terms of the Order in Council before reading the letter. The other Order in Council was
that the Controller should "investigate the cost of production of pulp, book and halftone papers." The letter is as follows:
Ottawa, Feb. 26, 1918.
Dear Mr. Pringle,
Following up the conversation I had with you yesterday I brought the matters we discussed to the attention of Council and the view of Council.was that the manufacturers should continue to supply the publishers with paper on the terms of the Orders in Council pending a final fixing of the price.
In the former Orders in Council was there not provision that the manufacturers should continue to supply the publishers whom they had been accustomed to supply with newsprint? Does this provision remain in force and still govern or should there be supplementary provisions covering this point?
I was also authorized by Council to say that it was not the intention of Council in passing the recent Order to authorize an investigation into the newspaper business. The intention of Council was only to authorize the completion of the investigatio'n you already have in hand. If the terms of the Order in Council as drawn up might embarrass you in dealing with the matter it can be amended so as to put beyond question the intention of the Council.
Yours faithfully,
N. W. Rowell.
R. A. Pringle, Esq., K.C.,
Paper Controller,
Ottawa.
As I understood the Orders in Council, and as the Government understood them, they did not authorize, and never were intended to authorize, an investigation into the newspaper business. Therefore, in the letter I stated what the intention of Council was as expressed in the Order.

Mr. Graham was commissioned in that month to undertake the task of speeding up the production of grain and cattle by the Indians in the three Prairie Provinces only, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. An appropriation of $300,000 was made to him for the purpose. I wish to give an account to the Bouse of what Mr. Graham has succeeded in doing with that appropriation. I can do so, I think, without taxing the patience of the House even at this very late and sensitive hour.
Mr. Graham's activities were in three spheres. First, came the establishment of what he terms Greater Production Farms.
Under that head he has so succeeded- and indeed, he just had one year to succeed in-that the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs is now the largest farmer in the Dominion. The Department of Indian Affairs has this year in crop of its own 30,448 acres of new land, all of which was broken last year with machinery owned by the department by men engaged by the department and under the charge of Mr. Graham. That land cost the country to break and make ready for crop an average price of $5.60 per acre,-and those who know anything about the breaking of land in Western Canada under present conditions will not make very much complaint as to what it cost the Dominion to break those 20,448 acres last year. I now come to the third sphere of activity, namely, the obtaining of the consent of the Indian to utilize unused land on his reserve for leasing for farming and grazing purposes. We pay the Indians for these surrenders, and we release for farming and grazing purposes these lands so surrendered, under specified conditions. By these operations a very considerable profit, indeed, will accrue to the department. Just what is to be done with that profit-indeed, we hhve the profit already-is not finally determined. The surrenders are taken only temporarily, of course; only for use during the time of the greater production activity. By this arrangement the Indian is the better off by the amount we give him for the surrender; the Government is the better off by the profit it makes in .connection with the business, and the country is better off by the production that accrues as a result of that policy. I shall be able to give the House at the next session some account of the production that actually does accrue this year as a result of Mr. Graham's activity in this third sphere of his work; it will be greater, in my opinion, than was the case in either of the other two spheres. But I have gone far enough to show that no more successful enterprise has ever been launched in Canada, or, up to the present time at all events, no better managed enterprise. The results will be good from the point of view of returns from the money invested; they will be better still from the point of view of the good resulting to the Indian, who is taking more interest in his
[Mr. Meighen.l
work than he did and is keeping busy instead of idle. But the greatest value of all accrues so far as the nation is concerned in the tremendous increase that Mr. Graham has been able to secure in the actual product of the soil upon those Indian reserves in Western Canada.
I believe that I have delayed the committee as long as I should at this period of the session, but had the time been earlier I would have done the credit to a very able and very devoted public servant that he well deserves by a much more detailed account of his operations in greater Indian production.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I think they are treaty Indians. Part of this item, $5,000, is required for the establishment of a hospital and six beds at Fort St. George, the headquarters of the Anglican Mission on the east coast of James bay and Hudson bay, to serve partially the wants of 1,600 Indians and Eskimo. The department is having difficulty in discharging its duty with regard to these Indians and Eskimo. Ever since the great fire of thirty-five years ago, the effect of which was to drive the caribou away into the interior of Labrador and toward the Newfoundland end of the Labrador peninsula, the Indians have found it almost impossible to subsist; the habits they have had to follow to make a living have impaired their health and they have been dying rather rapidly. An item of $5,000 is to take care of a herd of reindeer which has been taken over from

the Grenfell Association. The idea is that we establish a reindeer herd of sufficient size on the east coast of Hudson bay that ultimately will enable the Eskimo and the Indians there to get back to their original mode of life. It is the only mode that enables them to indulge in those habits which they have indulged in through so"many generations and which are, consequently, so necessary for their health.
Will they be allowed to kill the reindeer?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not for some time, except very few. We hope to multiply the herd; we are succeeding to some extent, end we hope to bring some more in.

I very much sympathize vith the habits of the Indian and love to see him enjoy his native haunts, but it would appear to me that if the old habitation of the Indian has been burned up, if the place has been rendered uninhabitable for the Indian in his usual habits, some effort should be made to take him away from there and put him somewhere else where he would become a useful citizen and, perhaps, farmer, as the Indians appear to be in the West. The minister has told us that the Indians have increased their production as farmers by 35 or 40 per cent, and as regards those Eskimos and Indians away back in Quebec or in the back settlements of that far-away region, would it not be better in the interest of humanity and along the lines of humani-tarianism for the department to take them away from there and put them in some better place?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: No, not bonuses; increases in pay, by reason of conditions. They did not have to follow the regular Civil Service routine and consequently could not claim a bonus on the same grounds as ordinary civil servants. I am very anxious to see the Dominion Police, who, to the best of my observation, are not only competent, but throughly devoted to the service of the State, get a fair remuneration.

Royal Northwest Mounted Police-To provide for one clerk in Third Division, subdivision B, at $700, $700.

This item is small in
itself, but it is important in conjunction with other matters. There is no objection to an item providing for one clerk in the Third Division but all through the list of the Supplementary Estimates provision is made for large additions to clerical staff. It has been repeatedly said in the House, apparently with good authority, that the Civil Service is overmanned, and we have a report made by a committee of the House representing that there is a considerable overmanning of the public service. Yet, we find again and again a number of extra clerks being provided for. We find in the office of the Governor General's secretary, two clerkships, in the Department of Justice, three clerkships; in the Department of the Secretary of State, six clerkships; in the Department of Immigration and Colonization, two clerkships; one clerkship in the Department of Indian Affairs; and in this item another one is

Then there are eight clerkships in the Department of Agriculture, and in the Department of Railways and Canals three clerkships; in the Department of Trade and Commerce, fourteen clerkships. The Department of Labour has no fewer than seventeen clerkships. I do not profess to have any knowledge as to the need in any particular case, but it is a curious fact that when we have a report to the effect that the Civil Service is overmanned scores of new clerks are being appointed.	*

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All these places must be filled by the Civil Service Commission. It is the view of the Government, communicated to the Civil Service Commission that where vacancies occur in any department they should be filled as far as possible by available persons from other departments without bringing in outside clerks. But the question as to where a clerk should come from is finally settled by the Civil Service Commission. The Government asked all the departments to furnish a list of clerks in their respective departments who could be dispensed with, and these lists were furnished the Civil Service Service Commission in order that they might, in filling positions where

vacancies occur, draw from the existing staffs rather than bring employees from the outside.
Take the case of the Department of Labour, which is to have 17 new clerks.	*
I gave last evening the explanation of the increase in this department. I am sorry I have not my notes here to refer to.
That item is not under consideration, I admit.

My impression is that the work of the department has been considerably extended during the past two or three years, and it is desired to make permanent appointments to the positions which have been temporary.

Has the department not been relieved by the transfer of the Statistical Branch to the Department of Trade and
Commerce?

No, the Statistical Bureau was under the Department of Agriculture, and that has been removed to the Department of Trade and Commerce. There has been an increase in the clerkships in the Department of Trade and Commerce due to the fact that the Bureau of Statistics has been extending its operations and giving the public more diversified and extended statistical information. I think these clerks were all necessary. In connection with the Bureau of Statistics Branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, created two years ago, the work has been carried on by temporary provision and a vote this year has been taken to provide for permanent employments.
Has not the branch of the Department of Labour, which had amongst its duties to ascertain the cost of living, been transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce? '
I think the Statistical Bureau proposes to do most of the work for the Department of Railways and Canals hereafter.
I am talking about what has been done.
I would not like to say that the Statistical Bureau are doing that work now. I think they are doing some. The Department of Labour is not a department that is overmanned in any respect.

I am not saying that, but I remember having heard the statement in the House last year or the year before last that the Department of Trade and Commerce was taking over the Statistical Branch and that part of the work done in the Department of Labour was being turned over to the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I do not desire to criticise any particular department, but we have the main facts before us that the service is admittedly overmanned, and yet we are going to ut on a lot of new clerks. If we were given the assurance that these vacancies are going to be filled by transfers from branches which are overmanned, that would be a reasonable explanation; but I would advise my hon. friend not to give a guarantee as to that because the Government might have difficulty in living up to it.

I think it would be impudent to give the guarantee; but, notwithstanding, the advice of my hon. friend is well-founded. The statistical section of the Department of Railways and Canals is about to be closed and transferred to the statistical bureau of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Mr. McFall, who has been doing some work for the Department of Labour during the war, really belongs to the statistical bureau, and he will go back there. That is true of a great many other branches of the statistical work. I think there will be considerable diminution in the staff of the Customs by reason of the Department of Trade and Commerce taking over a good deal of the statistical work.

With the increase in the number of clerks, I am afraid we are not getting a corresponding increase in efficiency. I had occasion to ask for some statistics recently, and there was very little that I could get. I wanted to find out what was the total amount of the succession duties collected in the various provinces, and also the appraised value of the estates in those provinces. The statistical branch was not able to give me the appraised value of the estates in Canada from which succession duties have been collected. I thought that was a very poor showing by a branch which is supposed to collect statistics. The fact that we may want at some future time to levy taxation on estates indicates to my mind that this is a matter that might engage the attention of the statistical branch. There are no very com-

plete returns, as far as I could find out, to be got in that branch. It has been my experience when I asked for information to find that it was not available-not always, but very often. No one objects to proper support of the statistical branch, if we were assured that we would get the value for our money. In reference to the point raised by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) the growth in the number of officials is alarming, in so far as I can judge. I drew to the attention of the House the other night the fact t-ha't the cost of civil government has grown from something like $4,000,000 to $6,000,000 within the last few years. There ought to be some check put upon that. There are expenditures being made that are not remunerative and are therefore not justified. I could refer to some of them, for example, the Department of Public Information. We are absolutely wasting money, in my judgment, upon that department. I asked a question in the House not many days ago as to what it was costing and-would you believe it, Mr. Chairman-they are spending $7,400 a month on the Department of Public Information. That is $240 a day, or $10 an hour. While my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) is asleep, this expense is going on. If he slept eight hours last night, there was $80 of the people's money spent while he slept, and if he took another hour this morning to bath and say his prayers that would be $10 more.

In connection with this
item I would like to say a word or two with regard to the department. For some time, as I understand it, the member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) was Parliamentary Secretary for the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Department, and after he had held the position for five or six months he resigned. Within the last few weeks another gentleman, who was at the head of the Medical Department, also resigned, giving pretty much the same reason as that given by the hon. member for Colchester. I would like to draw the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, to one paragraph in the letter of resignation of Dr. McKelvey Bell. It reads as follows:
Under the circumstances, the retention of my present position as Director of Medical Services would he a tacit admission of concurrence in principles against which 1 have made the stronges possible protest. I have always felt that unless the organization of the department were placed upon a sound and economic basis, it could not continue to operate indefinitely or successfully.
I have not before me a copy of the letter which was sent to the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Colchester when he resigned, but I understand that in that letter the hon. member stated that he had *been waiting for five or six months in order that his duties should be defined, and when he found no action was being taken upon his application he resigned. We have not had the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) or from the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn), the minister responsible for that department, any explanation as to the causes which led to these resignations; that is to say, what the department have to state concerning the matter. I think it is time now that this item is before the committee to hear from the Government something concerning this matter, which is of vital interest to the entire country. May I say that in an editorial published in the Montreal Gazette,-a journal which I understand is not inimical to the Government -the following occurs:

In his letter of resignation, Eieut.-Col. F. McKelvey Bell, Director of Medical Services for the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establish- ment, criticizes the conduct of what has become an important branch of the public service. His views on medical organization have been, he states, at variance with the system established under the late Military Hospitals Commission, and which, or much of it, was continued in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. Although the department is concerned only with sick and disabled soldiers, the medical service has been made secondary to almost every other branch of the organization " and has become merely one cog in an unwieldy machine." For this state of affairs Ool. Bell is not disposed to assume any personal responsibility. On the contrary, he states that recommendations made by him, looking to greater degree of unity and increased efficiency, have been disregarded or given only cursory consideration. He charges a lack of sympathy and understanding of medical requirements and even " antagonism to the profession generally," and finding his position an impossible one, he takes what, if his criticisms are well-founded, is the only course left open to him; he resigns.
A little later in that editorial-I do not intend to read it all-occurs the following:
The tenor of Col. Bell's letter of resignation is curiously similar to that in which Mr. F. B. McCurdy resigned as Parliamentary Secretary to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment last September. Read together the two communications create an impression that is disturbing. (Mr. McCurdy complained that his duties had never been defined, although a period of nearly seven months had elapsed', and that for many months no meeting of the Hospitals Commission had been held. He was unwilling to accept responsibility where he could exercise no authority, and he resigned.
Now, I understand with regard to this Soldiers' 'Civil Re-Establishment Department that something like fourteen hundred officials have been employed without the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. I should like to know from tbs' minister if those are the facts, and, generally, we should like to have from him some further details respecting the matters which I have brought before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In reference to the last statement of my hon. friend, that some fourteen hundred officials had been appointed without the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, I am informed there is no foundation for it. The officials of the Department of Soldiers Civil ReEstablishment are appointed by
10 p.m. the Civil Service Commission the same as in the other Departments of the Government according to my information. With respect to the other matter mentioned, the resignation of Dr. McKelvey Bell, the Prime Minister himself laid the correspondence upon the Table and is looking into it. I have no personal knowl-
4Mr. Jacobs.]
edge of the matter. But, speaking generally with reference to the work of the Department, my hon. friend will realize, and the members of the Committee will realize, that the work of this Department is something entirely new-it is breaking new -ground in all sections of Canada and undertaking a very difficult piece of work.
Officers interested in similar work in Great Britain, France, and the United States representing the governments of these countries have all recognized the excellent manner in which the work has been planned in Canada and the results which are being secured. Representatives from Great Britain, France, and the United States have visited Canada with a view to inspecting the -work now being carried on under this Department, and these representatives have, quite in an unsolicited way, written to the officers of the department bearing testimony to the very efficient character of the work. I submit that such testimony is evidence that so far as our work is concerned, compared with that carried on in other countries, we are doing exceedingly well.
Had they read Mr. McCurdy's letter at that time?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know if they had had the advantage of reading that letter.
Or Dr. Bell's?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They may not have had the advantage of reading Dr. Bell's letter either. But they did have the advantage of seeing the work carried on, and that was their testimony. It is a tremendous task, as my hon. friend will realize, and it would be surprising if some mistakes were not made in developing a new type of work all over the country where large staffs must be employed; but, as I say, the testimony from independent sources is that the work is highly satisfactory and the results secured, according to the information furnished me, indicate that the work is efficient, and that the men who have secured positions after leaving the retraining establishments of the department have proved efficient in the industries they have entered.

The hon. minister states that the fourteen hundred officials to whom I have referred were appointed through the Civil Service Commission. I am instructed that those officials were appointed first by the department, and approval was sought from the Civil Service Commission

afterwards. I would like to know if that is a fact or not.
Mr-. ROWELL: What I understand is that so far as the headquarters of the department is concerned and the staff here, they have all been appointed through the Civil Service Commission, as I intimated to my hon. friend.
