speechtext: I do not know that it was after they had been appointed.
After they had started their duties?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In cases where the department needed certain staff in the outlying districts, they did, because the Civil Service Commission did not have an eligible list of men available for the particular type of work to be carried on, hunt up persons whom they believed to be suitable, and submitted the names to the Civil Service Commission. The Civil Service Commission approved those names.
How long after they had entered upon their duties?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand that the
names would be immediately submitted to the Civil Service Commission. My hon. friend will see that this work is of an emergent character. This department must be in a position to deal promptly and efficiently with men who come to them for treatment, as do thousands after their discharge from the army. If a man is suffering from some incurable disease or from an injury from which early recovery is not expected, he is discharged from the service and is passed on to the Department of Soldiers1 Civil Re-Establishment, which, in addition to carrying on the work of retraining, deals with all incurable and tuberculous cases. The department must have staffs at all the outlying centres in order to deal with the men who are sent to them for their care, and they must secure such officials as they require for that purpose. I understand that these are the conditions under which these officials were secured.

The minister will not deny the statement I make that 1,400 officials were employed and that the approval of the Civil Service Commission was not
sought until some considerable time after these men had entered upon their duties.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No; that is not my understanding of the situation. I have already explained my understanding of it, and it is of record on Hansard.

I understand that there are three medical departments working concurrently, and in many cases overlapping. One department is under the Charge of the Canadian Army Medical Corps, of the Militia Department. Then there is the department over which Colonel McKelvey Bell presided; and the cause of his resignation was that the department sought to appoint an executive in connection with medical work who would not be responsible to Colonel Bell. I would like to know whether that is the fact and what the minister has to say respecting it. N Mr. ROWELL: My hon. fiiend is again in error in his presentation of the situation so far as he refers to overlapping. The work of the Army Medical Service, under the Department of Militia, is entirely distinct from the work carried on by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. The Army Medical Service deals with the man so long as he is a soldier and deals with hospitals in which soldiers only are treated. But if a man requires further treatment after his discharge he comes' under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, and as the Department of Militia and Defence ceases to require particular hospitals for the treatment of soldiers, these hospitals are transferred to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. There is no overlapping in the work; one staff looks after one set of hospitals and another staff looks after the other. There are not two separate services; the Army Medical Corps looks after soldiers; the Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment Department looks after men who, after their discharge, require further treatment.

I understand that one of the reasons for Colonel Bell's resignation was that the department was seeking to estaulish in the department an entirely new medical service, not to be responsible to Colonel Bell, but to work independently of him.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My information is that Colenel Bell is incorrect in making that statement; that the department did not want to establish an entirely separate branch. They wanted to keep it all in one branch.
The minister admits that there are two departments treating the soldiers medically, does he not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I do not. There is one department treating soldiers; there is another department treating men after their discharge.
They are soldiers. Mr. ROWELL: Not after discharge.
Why should we have two departments dealing with the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Because one deals with the man as a soldier; the other deals with him after discharge. After he is discharged from the army he is no longer a soldier, and the Department of Militia has nothing further to do with him.
How many returned soldiers are included among the 1,400 officials that I mentioned this evening?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: If I remember correctly, the press stated that before he resigned Colonel McKelvey Bell demanded of the Government a salary of $10,000 and that the Government refused to accede to that request. Is there any truth in that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed that in
the correspondence which the Prime Minister laid before the House jvas a letter from the minister of the department in which that fact was set forth.

Is the minister aware that in answer to that charge, Colbnel Bell said: "It is a clever misrepresentation of the facts?" I may say just here that it is rather significant that the member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy), although he has been in this House for the last five months, has never seen fit to take up the question of his resignation and to air it in the House.
Is that because some official chloroform has 
been administered, to him or what is the reason?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) is very well able to look after himself without the assistance of my hon. friend.
The fact that he is able to look after himself and is not doing so is, to my mind, a little significant.

I was under the impression that the public generally had a clear enough comprehension of the reasons that impelled my resignation, and I have had no intention of referring further to the matter. But the way my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) puts it, I must assure him there is no reason for silence on my part. No one has ever suggested any curtailment of expression. As the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) may not be aware, but as I am sure hon. members of the House generally are aware, shortly after my resignation as Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment was accepted, I was interviewed by a press representative and expressed in a general way the reasons for my retirement. At that time I stated it was "inaction." If I must be more specific at the present time, I perhaps had better read the official correspondence which passed,, part of which was talked of earlier in the session. The correspondence opens in September, 1918, by this letter which I wrote to the Prime Minister:
Ottawa, September 17, 1918. The Right Honourable,
Sir Robert Borden, P.C., M.P.,
Prime 'Minister,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir Robert:
On February 21st I read an official Ottawa news despatch in the Montreal Star stating that on that day a department of soldiers' civil
re-establishment had been created with	
	and F. B. McCurdy as Parliamentary
Secretary.	.
On the following day I called on you and Sir James Lougheed and learned that the report was correct, and that it had been decided that I should succeed Sir James as Chairman of the Military Hospitals' Commission operating under the name of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission.
On the following Monday I was furnished with a copy of P.C. 532 creating the Department of
Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment with	
and a Parliamentary Secretary " who shall have and perform such powers and duties as the Governor General in Council may from time to time prescribe."
No definition of these powers and duties was ever prescribed at that time or since, and in absence of such I of course then assumed that so far as office or executive activities between Sessions of Parliament were concerned I should carry on as Chairman of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission.

On March 1st, Honourable J. S. McLennan, Chairman, Executive Committee, Military Hospitals Commission, wrote the commissioners enclosing copies of recent Orders in Council, and advised them that a meeting of the commission would shortly be called. This has not yet been done. In fact, no meeting of the Military Hospitals Commission has yet been held since November 16th, 1917.
Having failed to have a definite line of policy outlined in so far as it affects my field of activity in this department, I on August 9th made a formal request of the minister (see copy of letter attached) that the secretary be instructed to call a meeting of the commissioners at an early date, but no action ensued. Under these circumstances I have had an idle summer, and in the war period when it has been the natural wish of every one to be unusually busy, the department has absorbed my time, but not my energies, for there has, under the circumstances, been nothing to do.
If a period from February 23rd to date (nearly seven months) has not sufficed for the Government to define the duties of a Parliamentary Secretary of this very important department, or determine whether the Invalided Soldiers' Commission as a body is to live or die, it augurs badly for a prompt and effective treatment at the Government's hands of the great problems that this department must face. .
If the Government had all eternity to work out its after the war soldiers' problems and to discharge the country's obligations to its gallant defenders it would not matter, but a policy of drift, inaction and delay is particularly inept here.
I have given freely and gladly of my time and energies in connection with the Government's operations, as a Member of Parliament, Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence, and in this department, but I am unwilling to risk my standing and reputation, in being attached to an undertaking whose duties and responsibilities are so lightly regarded.
I therefore tender my resignation as Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers* Civil Re-Establishment and Chairman of the so-called "Invalided Soldiers' Commission."
The letter to Sir James Lougheed which was attached to the letter which I have just read reads:
Ottawa, August 9, 1918.
Sir James Lougheed.
Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, Ottawa.
Dear Sir James:
The evident intention at the time of its authorization was that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment should take under its wing the various activities connected with returned soldier problems, and the public will probably expect the department, where it does not already possess the power, to move towards securing control over existing agencies and such extensions as time and experience demonstrate are necessary. In short, the returned soldier problem is on the department.
I have been anxious for some time past that a meeting of the Military Hospitals' Commission Commissioners should be called, at which you would formally advise them of the changes made and indicate in a general way what the future policy of the commission would be. I believe an intimation was conveyed to the commissioners by a member of their executive shortly after the name was changed to the effect that a meeting would be held at an early date. The secretary has, however, not yet sent out a notice.
As soon as you have acquainted them with the changes, the way would be clear for me to assume the duties of Chairman of the Commission. After full consideration I came to the conclusion that the best method of procedure is that the services formerly carried on by the Military Hospitals Commission should be continued through the medium of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission.	There would be no
change whatsoever in the personnel of the commission, but at their first meeting under the name of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission they should pass a resolution putting all executive power out of their hands.
Inasmuch as the Government, through the department, would be directly responsible to Parliament and the country for the Invalided Soldiers'	Commission expenditure it must
through its nominees exercise executive direction, but the commissioners with their interest in returned soldiers could by observation arid advice render excellent public service in an advisory capacity, which they would doubtless be glad to do.
I would therefore ask, if you concur, that the secretary be instructed to call a meeting of the commissioners at an early date.
Under date of November 7, Sir Robert Borden wrote me as follows:
Ottawa, Ont., November 7, 1918. F. B. McCurdy, Esq.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. McCurdy:
Since you conveyed to me, in the latter part of September last, your desire to be relieved of your duty as Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, I have had the opportunity of discussing the matter with you on two or three occasions when I expressed the desire and hope that you would reconsider your proposal and continue your duties as Parliamentary Secretary. It is with much regret that I learned finally your decision to retire, and it is only just that I should express to you my appreciation of the patriotic devotion and high sense of duty, as well as the conspicuous ability with which you have carried on your work in the Department of Militia and Defence, and in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment. In retiring from the position which you have held during the past seven months you take with you the best wishes of all the members of the Government, who are fully conscious, as I am, of your fine service and the patriotic purpose which alone animated it.
Believe me,
Tours' faithfully,
R. L. Borden.
The matter of my resignation was, I take it, referred to by the Minister of the Department of. Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment for his comments, because among the papers-

The hon. member has not, read the reply to the letter of August 9,

to Sir James Lougheed, or was there a reply?
I stated in my letter of September 17, to the Prime Minister that no reply had been received.

As yet?
Mr. MoCURDY: None, up to that date, and, of course, none since. And I advised the Prime Minister no action had been taken.
Does the hon. member say that he wrote a letter of resignation to the minister under whom he served, and that there was never 'any reply to it?
If the hon. gentleman will hear the rest of the correspondence-
I am not pressing for the letter. I am simply asking whether a reply was received acknowledging his letter of resignation, and if so, what was the reply?

The leader of the Opposition will realize that the position of Parliamentary Secretary is not that of secretary to a minister but Parliamentary Secretary to a department. Consequently, the appointment is made by Order in Council and the resignation when made is not addressed to the minister.
But the Parliamentary Secretary is in the department, and, I take it, he is subordinate to the minister of that department.
Yes, he is; but the letter of resignation properly goes to the Prime Minister.

Has a reply been received from Sir James Lougheed?
Mr. MoCURDY: No. I stated in my letter to the Prime Minister that I had received no reply to my letter to Sir James Lougheed, dated August 9th, and that no action was taken upon it. I learned by a return which was laid on the table of the House that Sir James Lougheed wrote to the Prime Minister, under date of November 15, 1918, as follows:
My -dear Sir Robert,
Answering the letter of your secretary, dated 6th November, 1918, touching Mr. McCurdy's resignation as Parliamentary Secretary of this department (dated September 17th) I beg to say that this Is the first intimation I have had of his resignation being based upon the reasons mentioned in his letter.
Although I was almost daily in communication with him, and though I knew he .was not in accord with the policy of the Government

on certain questions, yet he never suggested that there was any difference between us upon whiich he contemplated basing his resignation. He did suggest to me, in August last, that a meeting should be called of the Military Hospital Commissioners. His suggestion did not appeal to me inasmuch as my view was that such a meeting should be postponed, pending further consideration being given to the constitution of the commission both as to number of members and duties. This view was based on the following:
When the commission was organized in the summer of 1915, it was proposed to be limited to a commission of six (6) members: Through pressure being brought to bear upon the Government, it was finally increased to twenty odd. As the commission was administrative, this large number rendered it unwieldy in the transaction of its business duties.
On the 31st March last, the Government yielded to the persistent demand of the Department of Militia and Defence for the control of the commission's institutions and forty-one institutions operated by the commission for the care and treatment of convalescent soldiers, representing 12,359 beds, were handed over to the Militia Department. This was owing to the strong pressure brought to bear upon the Government by . the Canadian Army Medical Corps (a branch of the Militia Department), which contended that this was peculiarly work that should be placed under their charge. It will thus be seen that almost the entire work for which the commission was organized and administered was transferred to the Medical Branch of the Militia Department, thus relieving the commission of the duties for which it had been chiefly created.
The Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment was then created for the purpose of carrying on a work largely distinct from that for which the commission had been originally organized.
I have pointed out to Mr. McCurdy that in view of a new department having been created, and the work of the commission have almost entirely passed over to the Militia Department, our first duty would be to complete the organization of the various duties with which the department had been charged before taking action as to the calling together of the commission. I pointed out that under the Order in Council the commission had large administrative powers and that it would be an anomaly to have a commission and a department both exercising administrative powers within the same sphere of action. Manifestly it was necessary that the first consideration was the working out of the departmental organization, so that there would be no overlapping of duties between the two bodies.
I further suggested that as practically all of the members of the commission had forwarded their resignations some time previously, in my judgment, it would be undesirable to take any step toward calling the commission together until we had clearly determined upon what the relation of the commission and the department should be to each other.
As I had been chairman of the commission from its organization in 1915 down to March, 1918, I was in a position to know that the situation had so changed as to render it undesirable to have a commission of twenty odd fnembers attached to a department until there was a clearly defined sphere in which it could

act without coming into conflict with the administration of the department.
Furthermore, there was nothing which a commission could then do and had the commission been called together they would naturally have required to he charged with duties and responsibilities. Their former duties and responsibilities had practically passed over to the Militia Department and up to that time, I was unaware of any defined sphere of work that could be assigned to a commission. Mr. McCurdy had no suggestion to make of any active work or duties in which they could engage, and the calling together of the commission would not have furnished him with any additional employment that could have been of value. By Order in Council, he was appointed chairman of the commission and had he pronounced views upon the subject, there was nothing to have stood in his way, as chairman, in calling together the commission. I, of course, recognized his courtesy in discussing with me the whole subject and though I did not agree with his suggestion, this would not necessarily have stood in the way of his exercising his right, as chairman, to call together the commission.
Ais to Mr. McCurdy's complaint that there was no definite line of policy outlined as to a field of activity for him in the department- this, I may say, was not in my power to define. If the Order in Council did not define his duties, it would have been rather presumptuous for me to suggest to him what clearly would not have been within my authority.
During the time Mr. McCurdy was in the department, I was under the impression that he and his staff were kept busy. They seemed to be so engaged during that period and I regret very much if, owing to my views having differed from his upon the subject of the commission, the Government has been deprived of that work of activity which Mr. McCurdy complains he had not been given an opportunity to enter upon.
In conclusion I may say that during his connection with the department, the personal relations between us were of the most pleasant character, and therefore. I the more regret that we should have parted company for any reasons that may have led to his resignation.
Believe me,
Yours faithfully, James A. Dougheed. The lit. Hon. Sir Robert Borden, P.C., G.C.M.G, Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
On perusing a copy of that letter I, of course, at once wrote to the Priime Minister. On March 19, 1919, I wrote as follows:
Dear Sir Robert:
Under date of 4th instant I have received from your Secretary a copy of the letter of Sir James Dougheed of l'5th November last with regard to my resignation as Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers' Civil ReEstablishment and Chairman of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission.
Where Sir James states, "he did suggest to me in August last that a meeting should be called of the Military Hospital Commission Commissioners," I assume he refers to my letter to him of August 9th, 1918 (a copy of which 1
sent you) but I feel that in fairness to me he should have been more explicit and stated that he had received my letter of August 9 th and that it only reiterated many similar requests made verbally and continuously from the time of my appointment.
In stating that I might have called the Commissioners together it is possible that iSir James overlooked P.C. No. 446 passed subsequently to my appointment as Chairman, which Order in Council reads,-
" The Committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Right Honourable the Prime Minister advise that the invalided . Soldiers' Commission be under the direction and control of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment."
But apart from the necessity of my having the minister's authority to really operate as Chairman, I would regard it as only courteous to him to have his consent to oali the commissioners together under the changed conditions; besides it was obviously a courtesy due the Commissioners who had made many sacrifices to do public service, that he should meet with them and, as retiring chairman, explain the matters detailed in his letter to you, and genera ally to confer and collaborate with them in the new circumstances touching the affairs and welfare of returned soldiers in which they had so long been mutually interested. I should have thought that an explanation of the necessity of the changes was due to those public spirited citizens and the delay in that regard on the part of Sir James and his department was, in my view, most embarrassing, unfair and unbusinesslike. Personally, I did not realize until perusing the letter above referred to that I was being appointed as chairman of a defunct commission: it was certainly not complimentary to me, and I am confident that you would not be a party to such a proposal; but as to his own appreciation of the circumstances, I should have preferred his frank avowal at a much earlier date.
I do not think I need say anything further regarding my appointment as Parliamentary Secretary beyond referring to the Order in Council creating the office, P.C. 432, wherein it is stated that the Parliamentary Secretary " shall have and perform such powers and duties as the Governor General in Council may from time to time prescribe."
When appointed Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence, my duties were specifically defined and, frankly, I must state that I looked to the Government and the minister charged with responsibility for conducting the Department to define such duties as I might be able to discharge, that in assum- ' ing activities I might not be subject to the challenge of any subordinate members of the staff. No one could be expected to direct effectively without authority.
In this connection I received a communication from Hon. J. S. McLennan under date of 17th Deoember to which under date of 2nd January I replied, and I enclose herein copies of these letters.
Sir James' very apparent innuendo that in assigning causes for my retirement I lacked candour is certainly unwarranted, and is quite foreign to his usually generous disposition. You, at any rate, know that where I have had suggestions which I thought would make for improvement of public policy I have not hesitated to advise you.

After my resignation was accepted I wrote the Military Hospitals' Commissioners, explaining what I had done and why I had been compelled to take action.
December 9th, 1918.
To all Military Hospital
Commission Commissioners,
Dear Mr. On February 21st last I read an official Ottawa news despatch in the Montreal Star stating that on that day a Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment had been created
	" and F. B. McCurdy as Parlia-.
mentary Secretary
On the following day I called on the Prime Minister and Sir James Lougheed and learned that the report was correct, and that it had also been decided that I should succeed Sir James as Chairman of the Military Hospitals Commission operating under the new name of the " Invalided Soldiers' Commission This was duly embodied in an Order in Council.
On the following Monday I was furnished with a copy of P.C. 432 creating the Department of Soldiers' -Civil Re-Establishment and providing for the appointment of a Parliamentary Secretary " who shall have and perform such powers and duties as the Governor General in Council may from time to time prescribe ". But up to the present, so far as I am aware, no duties and powers have been defined.
A later Order in Council was passed placing the direction and responsibility for the operation of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission upon the Minister. With its passage, naturally the newly appointed Chairman could only proceed with the consent and approval of the Minister.
Inasmuch as the organization established by the Military Hospitals Commission was, in some form or other, to be taken over as a going concern by the new Department, I at once requested the Minister to authorize the Secretary to call a meeting of the Military Hospitals Commission Commissioners at which the Minister would outline the reasons for the creation of the Department and state along what lines it was desiraJble to operate and intimate in what capacity, if any, the Commissioners would be asked to carry on.
To me that appeared to be the first thing to be done and out of courtesy, if for no other reason, it seemed to me that the Commissioners should be at once called together. My own position was uncertain and undefined, and the Commissioners' status was equally anomalous until further considered and determined. I had been appointed Chairman by Order in Council * and I naturally desired to know the Commission and its functions as well as my own.
In March I was unofficially advised that a member of the Executive Committee of the Military Hospitals Commission had communicated to all the Commissioners that such a meeting would shortly be held, and it has no doubt been unsatisfactory to all concerned that nothing further ever came of the suggestion.
Whatever the merits of the organization and work of the Military Hospitals Commission have been, it must be recognized that the Commissioners had freely given of their time and energy and were doubtless anxious to promote the best interest of that branch of the public service. The problems of the Department and the Civil Re-Establishment of returning men were great and required profound consideration, study and treatment. And, apart from the 
necessity of first determining the Commission's own status and functions, I should have welcomed an exchange of views and the fullest collaboration in regard to all these matters at once, and long before the advent of Peace, when the larger numbers would be returning to Canada.
I had repeatedly requested the Minister to cause the Commission to be convened and as nothing was being done to that end, I formally wrote him on the 9th of August requesting that a meeting be called, but still no action ensued.
As this method of dealing with important urgent matters was foreign to all my previous business training and experience, and no action having been taken in response to my request, I forwarded my resigation to the Prime Minister on September 17th. It was accepted on November 7th.
Yours sincerely,
F. B. McCurdy.
December 9th, 1918.
Sir James Lougheed,
Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir James:
As I have been given some publicity as Chairman of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission and have received an enquiry from one of the Commissioners as to the reasons for my withdrawal, I have decided to write all of them whose addresses I can recollect. While doing so, I desire to furnish you with a copy of my letter to them, which you will, find enclosed.
Yours sincerely,
Senator McLennan's letter to me, just referred to in my letter of March -, 1919, to the Prime Minister, was the only communication received from any Military Hospitals commissioner that did not approve of my action. As it, inferentially, possibly questions that action, I shall read it:
Dear Mr. McCurdy,-
X have read with attention your statement of the course of events during the past summer, a considerable part of which time I was, as you know, absent from Ottawa.
I agree with you that as regards the Military Hospitals Commission and its successor, the course of events has not been satisfactory to the Commissioners.
I feel, however, that X should point out that you have taken a view different from mine as to the relative importance of deflning the status of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission as compared with the getting into operation the Department of Soldiers' CiviJ Ke-Efetablish-ment. This Department has wider functions than those of the Commission and it was more important to organize it than to deal* with the Commission. Its importance has been emphasized by the termination of hostilities, and the subsequent return of our troops sooner than could then have been anticipated. This view is confirmed by the fact that as Parliamentary Secretary of the Department it was within the scope, as ordinarily defined, for you to deal with all these problems from the standpoint of that office as effectively as from the standpoint of Chairman of the Com-misssion.
The care of the invalided men was being carried on during this period of transition with an organization and on principles es-

tablished by the Commission. I have been familiar from the beginning with the work of the commission, and without claiming that that work was perfect, my attendance at the Interallied Conference where I met representatives of the Allied Powers, dealing with this question, and after a careful examination of the principal centres where this work was being carried on in Great Britain lead me to believe that the principles which we adopted in the beginning were absolutely sound, and that the success attained in carrying them out compares favourably with that attained by other countries. I found also that the course taken by Canada in the formation of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and of giving to the Army Medical Corps the charge of all active treatment hospitals, was in conformity with the views of most European experts, and which as I now view the Canadian problem were steps in the right direction for us.
J. S. McLennan.
F. B. McCurdy, Esq., M.P.,
Halifax, Nova Scotia.
To Senator McLennan I replied:
Ottawa, January 2, 1919. Hon. J. S. McLennan,
Invalided Soldiers' Commission,
Ottawa.
Dear Senator:-
I have your letter of 17th ultimo, forwarded to me from Halifax, and I am pleased to know that "as regards the Military Hospitals Commission and its successor, the course of events has not been satisfactory to the commissioners." I should not care to make any comparisons as to the relative importance of defining the status of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission and the getting into operation of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. My view is and always has been, and I think from a business standpoint it is quite sufficient, that both should have been established without delay. There surely can be no reason why they should not have simultaneously been organized effectively if those in full authority had so desired.
I must confess that I can hardly appreciate the reference contained in the third paragraph of your letter wherein you state,-
"This view is confirmed by the fact that as Parliamentary Secretary of the department it was within the scope, as ordinarily defined, for you to deal with these problems."
I cannot understand what is meant by "ordinarily defined." For my own part, I do not know what the term Parliamentary Secretary does mean unless it is specifically defined, and that officer is in fact impotent until there has been explicit definition of his duties, status and authority. In business operations I have aimed to be definite and, so far as I have been able, to deal promptly and effectively with business as it arises. Take the simplest illustration : In every corporation, society and organization the powers and duties of the president, secretary, treasurer and other officers are specifically stated in the constitution or by-laws, and it goes without saying that the more abstract and indefinite term of Parliamentary Secretary calls more loudly for definition inasmuch as it is dealing with public, not private business.
For your information I may say that when I was appointed Parliamentary Secretary of the Department of Militia and Defence my duties were definitely outlined at the time. And you are no doubt aware that when I was appointed Par-limentary Secretary of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment I naturally expected that my duties would be similarly determined, but on the contrary, according to P.C. 432 creating the department, they were restricted to "such powers and duties as the Governor General in Council may from time to time prescribe" and as no powers and duties were prescribed I was certainly left suspended in the air. So that your remark as above stated is without force because manifestly it is absurd to talk of overriding the Order in Council without which it would be impossible to function. Any other position would leave one open to attack by any subordinate, apart from considerations of propriety and constituted authority for his actions.
And with regard to the Invalided Soldiers' Commission, I may again remind you that when I was appointed as its chairman a further Order in Council was passed placing the commission under the direction and control of the minister. In the above circumstances, it could hardly be expected that any official, however anxious to perform public service with effectiveness or proceed with departmental work, could do so until both the Government and the minister of the department had taken fur-tner action, the former in defining the powers and duties of Parliamentary Secretary, and the latter in calling together his colleagues of the former commission and determining the 9tatus of the Invalided Soldiers' Commission. Nothing was done by either in the premises, and in the delay I, perforce, retired.
I feel assured that you will agree with me that I could not deal with problems over which I had no control, and in which I had, in effect, no status, until further action a6 indicated above had been taken by the authorities who alone could empower me to act, but who delayed and delayed and delayed.
Yours sincerely,
F. B. McCurdy. '
I have nothing to add to the correspondence. I trust that what I have said will be deemed sufficient.

Before we leave this item I would direct the attention of the ministers to the discussion which, the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) will remember, took place in the early part of the session, and if there is to be a reconstruction of the Cabinet, as we hear, I trust that those who remain in it will bear in mind that we have been urging upon the Government that there should be fewer departments controlled by members of the Senate. This important discussion to-night, and the interesting disclosures made by the hon. member for Colchester, all goes to show that the minister ought to be here to -answer for his conduct of a very important department. It is

hardly fair to expect that the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) can take the responsibility for all these things, and be able to answer for them. In these last hours of the session, speaking for the Opposition, I again urge the idea that in this democratic country the departments of Government should be represented by their official heads in this House and not by hon. gentlemen who are in another Chamber and who, however estimable they may be, are apart from us and not as amenable to the will and the wish of the people as representatives in this House.
Quarantine-Salaries and contingencies ot organized' districts ; public health in other districts ; Tracadie and D'Arcy Island Lazaretto, and Public Works Health Act, $241,00i0.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture; Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext:
During the year the services of the quarantine branch were transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Department bf Immigration and Colonization. Under the legislation put through this year all of this work will come under the Department of Public Health. The vote here is the same as last year. As I think I intimated in a letter I sent to the hon. gentleman, I have had an inquiry made with reference to all the services in connection with quarantine this year, and I have a report upon them. I propose to hand that over to the Department of Public Health when it is created, so that they may take such action as they think necessary. I am inclined to think that a good many changes could be made in connection with our quarantine service, but whatever I might have had in contemplation, I did not feel like taking responsibility of making them myself.

Public Works-Chargeable to capital-Marine Department, $10,000,000.	'
What does the minister propose to do with that money?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure that all hon. members of the committee are fully aware of the Government's programme for shipbuilding. The very modest amount that we have in this item is to complete the Government's programme.

Could the minister give us any idea what he expects to earn from his ships? I asked a question the other day about the rate earned on the cargo that the Warrior carried, and the answer I got was that it was not in the public interest to give us the information, and that at the end of the year a statement would he made by somebody to the shareholders-which is the Government-but that the people did not seem to have anything at all to do with it. The owners of ships in centres of business make no objection to the publication of the rates they receive for their freights. If you read the New York trade papers you will find the rates quoted day by day. I do not see any good reason why the minister should not give such information to a member of Parliament when he asks for it. The minister said, in the answer he gave to my former question, that he carried a certain amount of cargo from one port to another. He did not state the rate he received, and when he was asked to state it he declined to do so. In connection with this matter, I want to obtain from the minister, if I can, the rate that is being charged on raw sugar from the north side of Cuba to Montreal. I drew to the attention of the Minister of Railways some 11 p.m. time ago that I was informed that the Shipping Board of New York had made a rate for raw sugar from the north side of Cuba to New York at 384 cents per hundred pounds, and had made a larger rate to Halifax of 584 cents- 20 cents per hundred pounds more. It was a curious thing to me, that the Shipping Board of New York was fixing a rate on raw sugar to a Canadian city; that was the first point. Then it transpired that one of the Government's ships had been used for carrying sugar from Cuba to Montreal for the benefit of the Montreal refiners at 384 cents per hundred pounds,-the rate fixed by the Shipping Board of New York to New York,-whereas Montreal is twice as far away from the north side of Cuba as is Halifax; but the refiners at Halifax had to pay 584 cents per hundred pounds. I want information on two points:	In the
first place, is our Government willing to submit to the New YoTk Shipping Board fixing the rate to Halifax from the north side of Cuba? In the second place, is the Government using its ships to carry raw sugar for one particular concern at 20 cents per hundred pounds less than to their competitors in Halifax and St. John? I would like to get that information from either the Minister of Railways or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the reason I was unable to give the hon. member the information he asked for in regard to rates on cargoes carried by Government ships is due to the fact that these ships are being operated by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine under Mr. Hanna and his board of directors; it was with no desire on the part of the Government to withhold the information were we in possession of it.
I suppose, Mr. Hanna is a public servant, and if the minister does not know he could get the information by asking him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will be very glad indeed to get it.

What does the
Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) say? He is in charge of this business. I notice he smiles. He ought to be able to give me that information. I notified him a few days ago that I wanted to get it before the closing of the House.

The operation of the
ships has been by the Marine officials and under the board of directors operating the Canadian National railways. The rates made are kept by that company. Any information, of course, I would have to get from the board of directors, and I can get it if it is in the public interest that it should be given at any particular time. That is the only question that will have to be taken up and discussed at some future time-the question of giving information of that kind just at the time transactions may be made in connection with our great railway and steamship systems. This is what happens in connection with our railways and also with our steamships. Some person wants to get information that will be of assistance to him individually, and it would not be in the public interest to furnish it to him. I admit that members are entitled to all information that is in the public interest to impart, and I would suggest that at another session both sides get together and decide what information we should give out, for the reason that if it is against the apparent successful operation either of our steamships or our railways, I am sure there is not a member who would want the information. With reference to the rate mentioned, I do not know anything about it, but there has been in force on the Atlantic for years an understanding that the rates from Atlantic ports to foreign ports are the same whether from Canadian or United States ports.

The rate from Montreal to Liverpool would be the same as from Portland or from New York, and probably the rate from Cuba to Montreal would be the same as the rate from Cuba to New York. The matter of getting a return cargo has probably something to do with these rates being generally the same to the Atlantic ports.
Why are the rates higher to Halifax than they are to Montreal?	.
I will make inquiries and get the information.

The sugar rate from the British West India Islands, which enjoy preferential treatment under our West Indian Treaty, was fixed by the International Sugar Board. My impression is that the International Sugar Board fixed the rate on sugar from British West India Islands to Halifax and St. John at 57 cents.
Did they fix the rate to Montreal?

No, because during the war Montreal was getting its sugar via New York and the New York rate from the British West India Islands was somewhat lower because of the fact that the rail rate from New York to Montreal had to be taken into consideration. The, situation to which my hon. friend refers was unfair to the sugar refineries at Halifax and St. John, and as soon as I learned of it I protested. The Montreal sugar refineries wanted the Cuban sugar for the purpose of manufacturing it and selling it in the United Kingdom, and if the refineries at St. John and Halifax could not get the same rate as the Montreal people got, they were under a disadvantage in attempting to sell sugar in the United Kingdom. Later, however, I understand, the railway made the same offer to the refineries at St. John and Halifax as was made to the Montreal refineries.
I myself think that a mistake was made in the first instance.
My point is that the Government ships have been used for the benefit of the Montreal refineries and to the disadvantage of the refineries at Halifax and St. John.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I heard Mr. Hanna make the statement that he was quite prepared to carry sugar at the same rate to Halifax and St. John as he carried it to New York for the Montreal refineries.

The rate ought to be less from the north side of Cuba to 
Halifax and St. John than it is to Montreal, because it is only half the distance; but the rate to Halifax and St. John is 20 cents more than the rate to Montreal; and that is due to the interference of the Government. I am informed on credible authority that the Government have contracted- to carry
36,000	tons of raw sugar from the north side of Cuba to Montreal at 37} cents per hundred pounds. If that is true, it will be impossible for the refiners at Halifax and St. John to compete with the refiners in Montreal. The point is that the Government should not use Government ships to favour the Montreal refiners against the interests of the refiners at Halifax and St. John. If the minister cannot clear that point up, the people of the Maritime Provinces will not be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I thought I had made it quite clear. The Government have nothing whatever to do with the operating of the ships or the fixing of rates. The Government took care to see that just such a case as the hon. member has mentioned should not arise, as it possibly would arise if the Government operated the ships and fixed the rates. But the operation of the ships and the fixing of the rates is entirely in the hands of Mr. Hanna. The Government did not carry that sugar; the Government did not fix the rate; the Government had nothing whatever to do with it. If the facts are as the hon. member states, I am quite sure that the Minister of Railways will be glad to take the matter up with Mr. Hanna. But I know that the Minister of Railways, like all the other members of the Government, does not want to interfere with Mr. Hanna; we want to give him a free hand to operate the ships, just as we give him a free hand to operate the railways. But I did hear Mr. Hanna make the statement that he was quite prepared to carry raw sugar to Halifax and St. John at the same rate that he carried it to New York for the Montreal sugar refiners. Mr. Hanna would naturally be glad to get a return cargo, and sugar is about the only cargo he could get.

I understood that these ships were to be built for the advantage of the Canadian people, but we are told that the ships have been handed over to Mr. Hanna and that Mr. Hanna may do as he sees fit; that he may suit himself, not the Canadian people. It seems to me that we could do without this item of $10,000,000 if it is of no advantage to the people.

I am not quite satisfied with the explanation made by the Minister of Marine. He tells us that the management of the Government steamships has been handed over to Mr. Hanna; I suppose he means that it has been handed over to the Beard of Directors of the Canadian National railways, not to Mr. Hanna personally.
The Board of Directors, of which Mr. Hanna is President.

That is what I understood.
The Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) says that the Government have no control of the rates; that that is all left to Mr. Hanna; that the Government do not want to interfere with him in regard to the steamships, any more than with him in regard to the operation of the railways. We were told by the Minister of Railways last night that when any complaint was made with regard to railway rates those who were interested could appeal to the President of the Canadian National Railways, and if they were not satisfied with this decision they could make a further appeal to the Governor in Council, who would take the matter into further consideration and see that a decision was given which was in the interests of the public. If that is the case with regard to the Canadian National Railways, surely it ought to be the case with regard to the steamships built by the Government of Canada and operated by the Canadian National Railway Company.

These Government steamships have been handed over to the company of which Mr. Hanna is the President. Under our new Railway Act the Canadian National Railways come under the Board of Railway Commissioners the same as any other railway, and we have the right of appeal in these cases just as any other railway has. Some of our steamships may be under the Railway Act and thus come under the Board of Railway Commissioners. But the hon. member knows that in any case where an injustice has been done there is the right of appeal to the Governor in Council, through the Department of which I am the head, and any appeal so made will be taken up and dealt with with a view to doing justice to any hon. member who makes complaints, or to any individual. But until it comes before the Government in that way, of course, we leave the responsibility for chartering and operating those vessels as before. The only difference is this: You cannot fix a general rate as you can with the Board of Railway Cornmissioners. A vessel may arrive at Montreal, and you may want to charter it to China, Japan or Liverpool, and the rates may differ from time to time. I do not think it is easy to get a standard rate. I rose only to assure the hon. member that at all times there is the right to appeal to the Governor in Council, to the management of the vessels or to the minister himself in connection with either Government vessels or railways.

If the information which the hon. member (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has given to the committee to-night is correct, namely, that there has been this discrimination of 20 cents in the freight rate as between Montreal and Halifax and St. John, the Governor in Council should not wait for some one to make an appeal, but should take the matter in hand at once and see that justice is done.

The rate to
Halifax and St. John was not fixed by the Government steamships nor by the Board of Railway Commissioners; it was fixed by the International Sugar Commission which owns and controls all the sugar production of the British West India islands until next September or October, and in some way or another they control the freight. Two years ago they fixed the rate from the British West Indies to Halifax.

What has the
Government done to rectify this? Has the Government taken any action at all?
It could not be rectified because it is a rate fixed by an Inter-Allied Commission.

I understand the Board of Railu ay Commissioners, knowing that raw sugar was being taken to the sugar refineries at Halifax and St. John at 58i cents per 100 pounds, afterwards entered into a contract using Government ships, for which the people of Canada pay, and gave the benefit of that 20 cents per 100 pounds to Montreal, and that means that for the benefit of some people in Montreal, absolute disaster is threatened to those two enterprises in the Maritime Provinces each having an investment of some $10,000,000.

Unintentionally a discrimination was worked against the Halifax and St. John refineries. They presented their opposition to this to the railway. Then the railway undertook to place Halifax and St. John in the same position as regards Cuban importations of sugar.



A mistake was made, I think, in the first instance.
What steps are the Government taking, in the interest of the people, to correct that mistake?

The Government has had the matter up before the management of the Canadian National railways, and this matter has been placed before them. Parliament cannot correct it by discussing the matter here; it might well be left to the business interests involved and the good sense of the management.

In spite of what my hon. friend says, we are all interested. This is not a matter of whether I have money invested in that enterprise or not; I am interested just the same, and I do not think it is becoming to my hon. friend in a veiled way to insinuate that I have no right to discuss the matter here.
I do not say so.

That is what the hon. gentleman intimated, namely, that I had better leave the matter to the people who are directly interested. I am interested in this matter as a representative from the Maritime Provinces, and if a mistake has been made, while my hon. friend says that the matter has been referred to Mr. Hanna, that is all very well; that may be the proper way to get this matter adjusted, but when an item like this is before the Committee, people who are interested in enterprises in the Maritime Provinces, which enterprises are being driven out of business by circumstances which spell disaster to those enterprises, we should have some assurance from the Government that something will be done to see that those people are given a fair and proper settlement.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not want wrong information to get on Hansard. The Montreal Sugar Refineries applied to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine to move the sugar. They had to move it at the New York rate, and they did so. Had Halifax or St. John made the same application to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, they would have received the same rate. I am sorry to disagree with my colleague (Mr. A. K. Maclean), but there has not been any error. When the other two refineries make application, they will get the same rate. There is no discrimination whatever.

Then we are to conclude that there is to be nothing done to straighten

this matter out and to see that these incfus-tries in the Maritime Provinces are not discriminated against.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter has been arranged.
How?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I just stated a moment ago that Mr. Hanna is quite willing to move sugar at the same rate for St. John and Halifax, as soon as the industries in the Maritime Provinces ask him to do so.
Are vessels available to engage in the trade?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
The St. John refinery has already received a cargo.
Why did the minister not give me that information half an hour ago?
I heard this only about five minutes ago.

speechtext:

The problem is a large one, but Monday will decide whether there will be a modification in the. contract and the Government will go on with it, or whether the contract will be cancelled.

amount; it used to be $2,500.

Special allowance to Mr. Justice Duff, to cover expenses when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, $2,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) is not here, and I am sorry I am unable to give the explanation. If my hon. friend presses for it, I shall be glad to inquire into it.

If it is the policy of the department to remit fines there will be many applications.
297i	;

The hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) may be able to give us some information about it.
IMr. COWAN: I was never in court, was never fined, and I don't know anything about it.
Air Service, $250,000.

This is in connection with the Act passed this session creating an Air Board. The Minister of Customs is chairman of the board, with which is associated the Department of Marine and Fisheries. board, the care of machines, and drawing up regulations. It was first suggested that $500,000 would be required for the year, but the amount was cut down, and they think that $250,000 will more than cover it. It is only in the experimental stage as yet.

speechtext: It is partly in connection with the classification scheme. Further Supplementary Estimates 1919-20- Provisional allowance for the Inside and Outside Services of the Civil Service, to be paid to such persons and classes of persons, in such amounts and at such times as the Governor in Council may determine, $10,000,000.

In connection with this item, I would again remind the Govern-

ment-I have already brought the matter to the attention of the President of the Privy Council-that there are a great many messengers around the House who are expecting to participate in this bonus. Some were helped and some were not. I trust that they will all be treated equally under this vote.

I desire to give some information as to the operation of the railways and the money that will be required in connection with them during the present fiscal year. For the Canadian Northern Railway system the gross earnings will amount to $94,000,000 and the working expenses, including fixed charges, will amount to $103,946,000, or a loss of $9,946,000. The Government system's earnings, it is estimated, will amount to $37,321,485, and the working expenses $42,812,240, or a total loss on the Intercolonial and Transcontinental part of the Canadian National system of $5,490,755. That is the statement made at the beginning of the year. It is estimated that the loss on the Grand Trunk Pacific will be about $9,000,000, and the loss on the Canadian National Railway system as a whole, say, roughly, $19,000,000, or a total of $28,000,000. In leply to a question asked by a member last year, I would state that this estimate includes interest on all the Canadian Northern Railway system. There is nothing for interest on capital in connection with the Intercolonial or Transcontinental Railway system. Expenditure on the construction of betterments this year on the Canadian Government end will be $11,121,600. On railway equipment, rolling stock for the whole system, $20,000,000. That is the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial and Transcontinental. On the Canadian Northern system only we estimate $21,421,000, made up as follows: Western lines construction, $6,975,000; Western lines betterments, $4,479,000; Eastern lines construction, $2,082,000; Eastern lines betterments, $6,885,000; and general, $1,000,000. This means a total of $9,057,000 for construction, and $12,000,000 for betterments. The following is a summary of the moneys to be supplied to the Board of Directors to meet the expenditures enumerated: Loss, $28,000,000; construction on the Canadian Government Railways, $11,121,000; equipment, rolling stock, etc., $20,000,000; Canadian National Railway construction and betterments, $21,421,000, or a total of $80,542,000. These are the figures as estimated for the coming year.

Is the title of that rolling stock in the department?
	\

It is in the Canadian National Railway system and the Government is nominally owner of all stock. Contracts have already been given for locomotives for some $2,350,000; freight equipment, $8,650,300; passenger equipment, $4,450,000; or a total of some $16,555,000 odd.
What is the total investment in the railways and what are the liabilities?

The amount given last year is $438,000,000, which has been added to some $25,000,000 during the present year for loss and for equipment.
Port Nelson Terminals-$100,000.

There is an item of $100,000 in connection with the Port Nelson terminals, and in the Supplementary Estimates $300,000 for Hudson Bay railway construction. What work is it the intention to do in connection with these items this- year?

This vote of $100,000 is to pay for items in connection with the staff we have there and cleaning up around the terminals during the present year. I have put $300,000 in the Estimates to cover ties to finish the Hudson Bay railway. The rails will be taken from the main line where we are putting on new rails, and as soon as we get the ties and rails we intend to start the work on Hudson Bay.
Is it the intention to lay the rails this year?
If we get the rails and the men.

I do not think anything like $100,000 will be used for terminals this year, and considerably more than $300,000 will be needed on the other work if any rails are going to be laid. 1 would suggest that this be amended to add to this1 item the Hudson Bay railway.

We cannot amend the Estimates, but I will be glad to take the hon. gentleman's suggestion into consideration. The engineer will look into the matter and if his suggestion is practicable it might be carried out.

If my suggestion were adopted, there would be $400,000 for the whole proposition. You would need only a small amount for one part of the work and you could use the rest of the money in connection with the other. I would ask

the minister why it is not the intention to complete the railway this year. In last year's estimates there was an item of $1,000,000 for the completion of the railway. I understood at that time that it was the intention of the Government to complete the railway last year but for special reasons that were given it was not done, and I naturally supposed that if they did not complete it last year the same vote would be made this year. Why is this $1,000,000 not revoted?
I cannot say. The estimates are there.

It seems rather peculiar that a railway which has been under construction for such a long time and which is so nearly completed has not been finished. Only ninety-two miles of steel is necessary to complete a railway of four hundred and twenty-four miles, under course of construction since 1912, and on which $20,000000 has already been spent. Lands have been set aside, of which $28,000,000 worth has been sold, $13,000,000 having been already collected. The country is paying for the railway in this way and it seems strange to me that under these circumstances that railway should not be gone on with this year, when so many new enterprises are being undertaken.
For some years there have not been very much in the Estimates in connection with certain enterprises, but I notice on the same page as this that there are very material increases in the expenditures for the Welland Ship Canal and the Trent Canal. We are spending $20,000,000 on good roads, $25,000,000 for housing, and $10,000,000 for something else. These are entirely new enterprises, while this work has been under way for a number of years and it is almost completed. Now, it is being allowed to lapse. It is an uneconomical way of proceeding with the railway; it suffers severely by deterioration and the result will be a great loss to Canada and to the Government. It is very peculiar that expenditures in connection with other public works of a similar nature are being increased this year, while for this particular work which has been under way for so long a less amount appears in the Estimates than in any one year for some considerable time. If the Minister of Railways can explain that, I would like to hear him do so.
Resolutions reported and concurred in. WAYS AND MEANS-THE SUPPLY BILL.
On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) the House went into Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolved. That towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the Public Service for the financial year ending 31st March, 1920, the sum of $162,527,610.91 he granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
Resolution reported, and concurred in.
Sir THOMAS WHITE moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 181, for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service of the financial year ending the 31st March, 1920.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the first and second times, considered in committee, and read the third time and passed.
On motion of Sir Thomas White the House adjourned at twelve o'clock midnight.
